assessmentSummary.identity: Frog Rockback is a bilateral bent-knee, wide-kneeling quadruped hip rock-back. From supported hands and knees, set the knees comfortably wide with lower legs supported, rock the hips posteriorly through a comfortable range, then return under control. One repetition is one rock-back and return. It is not the unilateral straight-leg Adductor Rockback, a static frog stretch, standing lunge, Cossack shift, Copenhagen exercise, crawl, assessment, or forced end range.
currentCardFindings: Source 59 has a useful legacy description but omits an exact repetition cycle, comfortable-width rule, foot/support dimensions, accessibility contract, fatigue tracking, substitutions, calibration, and human-review status.
The prior Adductor Rockback family audit correctly classifies Frog Rockback as a separate bilateral bent-knee definition; this source materializes that deferred definition rather than merging it.
Three legacy YouTube URLs are preserved as unverified candidate media only.

proposedTaxonomy.laterality: bilateral symmetrical lower-limb base; record any asymmetry or side shift separately
proposedTaxonomy.intent: low-load comfortable hip/adductor-region access with controlled rock-return

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the assigned base and range stay controlled without symptoms or compensation

coachCues: Choose a comfortable knee width and assigned hand height
Keep hands and lower legs supported
Rock hips back slowly and return
Make the range smaller before forcing depth
athleteInstructions: Set up on hands and knees with knees comfortably wide
Breathe and gently move hips back
Stop before pinching, pain, or back rounding
Return to the start under control
Rest or narrow the position if quality changes

calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: No source establishes a unique Frog Rockback score, dose, recovery period, clinical outcome, or transfer effect.

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Materialize Frog Rockback as its own candidate-only bilateral bent-knee wide-kneeling definition. Treat knee width, foot orientation, hand height, range, tempo, and pauses as explicit delivery modifiers, not automatic new cards. Keep unilateral Adductor Rockback, static frog positions, standing lateral tasks, direct adductor-strength exercises, crawling, and assessments separate.

currentCardSnapshot.description: From a supported hands-and-knees position, set both knees comfortably wide with lower legs supported. Rock the hips posteriorly through a comfortable range, then return under control. One repetition is one rock-back and return. This excludes a unilateral straight-leg Adductor Rockback, static frog position, lateral lunge, Cossack shift, Copenhagen exercise, crawl, assessment, and forced end range.

claims: Frog Rockback is a bilateral, bent-knee, wide-kneeling quadruped rock-back: knees move to a comfortable wide position, the hips move posteriorly, then return under control.
It excludes the unilateral straight-leg Adductor Rockback, a static frog position, a lateral lunge, a loaded adductor-strength task, locomotion, assessment, and forced end range.
Wide bilateral knees, lower-leg support, quadruped hand support, and a posterior hip rock distinguish this candidate from straight-leg unilateral and standing alternatives.
Knee width, foot orientation, hand elevation, range, tempo, and pauses are explicit delivery modifiers only when the bilateral frog base and rock-return cycle remain intact.

evidence.sourceTitle: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb: Medial Thigh Muscles
claims: Record medial-thigh/adductor, hip, trunk, shoulder, wrist, knee, and lower-leg support roles as task anatomy; do not imply diagnosis or an isolated-tissue outcome.
A wide-kneeling position does not establish a universal hip angle, tissue target, restriction, or clinical conclusion.
The candidate action is controlled posterior hip travel from a stable quadruped frog base followed by a return; a completed repetition is one rock-back and return, not an uncontrolled sink or hold.
Keep the trunk organised and reduce knee width or range rather than creating range through lumbar rounding or a forced groin position.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Difficulty values describe only exact exercise complexity and physical demand, never participant skill, proficiency, age, or classification.
Wide-knee floor support, hip range, trunk organisation, and shoulder/wrist/knee support create a low-load but coordination-sensitive task; independent calibration remains required.

evidence.sourceTitle: Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals: a systematic review
claims: Acute stretching responses depend on type, dose, timing, and the subsequent activity; no universal readiness, recovery, or performance outcome is claimed.
Track repetitions, range, knee width, hand support, trunk compensation, symptoms, and downstream work rather than assigning a universal recovery rule.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: A clear stable floor or mat, enough space to exit the kneeling base, optional padding or elevated hand support, and communication are practical safeguards.
Selection is based on the assigned task and current workout inputs, not an exercise-card population or skill label.

evidence.sourceTitle: Acute Effects of Various Stretching Techniques on Range of Motion: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
claims: Stretching research does not establish a universal Frog Rockback dose, range, cadence, or readiness threshold.
Use a conservative quality-limited candidate dose and stop before knee, hip, groin, back, wrist, shoulder, or support symptoms or persistent compensation.
Exact instructions name the hand-and-knee base, comfortable wide-knee boundary, lower-leg position, posterior rock, trunk rule, return, and reset.
Use a smaller range or narrower knee position before forcing depth; do not turn the drill into a passive prolonged sink.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Appropriate instruction, supervision, environment, and progressive exposure are safeguards.
Stop for sharp or increasing pain, new neurologic/circulation/breathing/dizziness symptoms, unsafe support or surface, inability to restore quality, or participant request.

evidence.sourceTitle: Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals: a systematic review
claims: Use Frog Rockback only when the exact low-load wide-kneeling hip-access task fits session objectives and downstream demands; it does not promise injury prevention, treatment, or transfer.
Any change to base, knee width, hand support, range, tempo, dose, or substitution reruns selection, logistics, duration, fatigue, and validation.
Athlete support should show the base, small controlled rock-return, comfortable range option, breathing, self-check, and stop prompt in plain language.
Media accessibility, exact variant match, captions, quality, and safety remain unverified until human review.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Coach support should include floor/mat and exit checks, exact base verification, front-and-side observation of knee width and trunk, range/tempo logging, and escalation for unresolved symptoms.
Do not diagnose an adductor limitation or use a generic frog position as an automatic substitution.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Candidate accessibility supports include padding, elevated hands, stable hand contact, a still sequence, captions, transcript, audio description, clear stop instructions, and a reviewed substitution when floor kneeling is inaccessible.
These supports do not verify an individual’s readiness or make an inaccessible base acceptable.
The unilateral straight-leg Adductor Rockback has a different laterality, knee position, base, and primary task and remains a distinct definition.

A specified wide-knee frog base can accept knee-width, foot-orientation, range, hand-height, tempo, or pause modifiers; static frog positions, lateral lunges, Cossack shifts, Copenhagen work, and locomotion are not automatic substitutions.

Three inherited direct YouTube URLs are retained solely as unverified candidates; no playback, embedding, exact task match, captions, accessibility, quality, safety, reviewer, or approval claim is made.
Privacy-enhanced embed URLs are generated for the review workflow but remain non-embeddable until human verification.

alternateAssessments.name: Narrower-Base Frog Rockback
alternateAssessments.rationale: Knee width changes range and tolerance while preserving the bilateral bent-knee wide-kneeling rock-return identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Elevated-Hands Frog Rockback
alternateAssessments.rationale: Changing hand height changes shoulder/wrist loading and trunk angle while preserving the specified frog base and rock-return action.

alternateAssessments.name: Frog Rockback with Controlled Pause
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared pause changes cadence only when the base, range, and rock-return remain unchanged.

alternateAssessments.name: Adductor Rockback
alternateAssessments.rationale: A unilateral straight-leg lower limb and different laterality/base change the primary task.

alternateAssessments.name: Static Frog Stretch
alternateAssessments.rationale: A hold without an assigned rock-return cycle is a different primary action and dose.

alternateAssessments.name: Copenhagen Adduction Exercise
alternateAssessments.rationale: A direct adductor-strength task changes support, leverage, loading, fatigue, and progression requirements.
